passages.t: Bold as a lion, and the poor man with integrity
passages.happening:
“The wicked flee when no one pursues, but the righteous are as bold as a lion” (verse 1). ‘A land in rebellion has many rulers, but a man of understanding and knowledge maintains order’ (verse 2). A leader who oppresses the poor is like a driving rain that leaves no food (verse 3).

‘Those who forsake the law praise the wicked, but those who keep the law resist them’ (verse 4). ‘Evil men do not understand justice, but those who seek the LORD comprehend fully’ (verse 5). ‘Better a poor man who walks with integrity than a rich man whose ways are perverse’ (verse 6).

Wealth gained by interest and usury will end up with someone who is kind to the poor (verse 8). ‘Whoever turns his ear away from hearing the law, even his prayer is detestable’ (verse 9). ‘A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man with discernment sees through him’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
More than any other part of Proverbs, this chapter speaks of the law, torah, God's instruction. It also keeps asking what happens to a people when the wicked or the righteous hold power. The Hezekiah collection seems shaped with rulers and future rulers in mind, which fits its keeping by royal scribes. But its sayings reach everyone.

Verse 2 reflects real instability. The northern kingdom had a string of short-lived dynasties, with kings murdered and replaced, in its last decades before Samaria fell to Assyria in 722 BC. Readers in Hezekiah's Judah had watched that collapse from nearby.

The law forbade charging interest to a fellow Israelite in need. Lending at high rates was common across the ancient world, and it often drove poor farmers into debt slavery. Verse 8 says such wealth will not stay with the one who gathered it.

In verse 3 a ruler who oppresses the poor is like a storm that washes the crops away instead of watering them. Some interpreters read the Hebrew as a poor man who oppresses the poor.
passages.later: The law says, ‘Do not take any interest or profit from him, but fear your God, that your countryman may live among you’ (Leviticus 25:36). And the psalm speaks of the boldness of verse 1: “The LORD is my light and my salvation” (Psalm 27:1).
passages.asks: The righteous are bold as a lion. Ask what you are afraid of that a clear conscience would let you face. And ask whether you are more impressed by the rich man's confidence or by the poor man's integrity.

passages.happening:
‘When the righteous triumph, there is great glory, but when the wicked rise, men hide themselves’ (verse 12).

At the center of the chapter stands one of the Bible's clearest sayings about confession: “He who conceals his sins will not prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them will find mercy” (verse 13). ‘Blessed is the man who is always reverent, but he who hardens his heart falls into trouble’ (verse 14).

‘Like a roaring lion or a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a helpless people’ (verse 15). A leader without judgment oppresses, ‘but he who hates dishonest profit will prolong his days’ (verse 16). A man guilty of bloodshed will flee to the grave, and no one should hold him back (verse 17). ‘He who walks with integrity will be kept safe’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Verse 13 is rare among the proverbs for how directly it speaks of confession. It names two steps: confessing sin, and turning from it. And it promises mercy, not merely a better outcome.

Verses 12 and 28 are a pair. When the wicked rise, people hide. A whole community feels the character of those who rule it.

Verse 15 pictures the ruler of a helpless people as a roaring lion or a charging bear, two of the most feared animals in Israel's hills. Power without righteousness is a wild animal loose among the weak.
passages.later: The psalmist knew both halves of verse 13: ‘When I kept silent, my bones became brittle from my groaning all day long’ (Psalm 32:3). Then, ‘I acknowledged my sin to You and did not hide my iniquity’ (Psalm 32:5), and God forgave. John says the same: ‘If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness’ (1 John 1:9).
passages.asks: Whoever confesses and turns finds mercy. Ask whether there is a sin you have been hiding, and what it would cost, and gain, to bring it into the light. And ask whom you could trust to hear you as you do.

passages.t: Hard work, honest rebuke, and an open hand to the poor
passages.happening:
‘The one who works his land will have plenty of food, but whoever chases fantasies will have his fill of poverty’ (verse 19). ‘A faithful man will abound with blessings, but one eager to be rich will not go unpunished’ (verse 20). ‘To show partiality is not good, yet a man will do wrong for a piece of bread’ (verse 21).

‘He who rebukes a man will later find more favor than one who flatters with his tongue’ (verse 23). A son who robs his parents and says it is no crime is a companion of the destroyer (verse 24). ‘He who trusts in himself is a fool, but one who walks in wisdom will be safe’ (verse 26).

“Whoever gives to the poor will not be in need, but he who hides his eyes will receive many curses” (verse 27). And ‘When the wicked come to power, people hide themselves; but when they perish, the righteous flourish’ (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Verse 21 is honest about how cheaply justice can be bought: for a piece of bread.

Rebuke and flattery mattered in public life, especially at court. Verse 23 praises the person willing to correct someone, even if they are not thanked at first.

Verse 24 condemns a son who takes from his parents and calls it fair, perhaps by seizing the family inheritance early or by refusing to support them when they are old.

Verse 27 is the closing word on the poor. To hide one's eyes is to look away on purpose.
passages.later: The psalm speaks of the one who does not look away: “Blessed is the one who cares for the poor; the LORD will deliver him in the day of trouble” (Psalm 41:1).
passages.hard:
Verse 27 says whoever gives to the poor will not be in need. Is that a promise that generosity always pays?

Read that way, verse 27 would become a kind of prosperity formula: give, and you will never lack. But it is a proverb, and proverbs describe how life usually goes under God, not a guarantee for every case.

Generous people tend to live among others who know them and help them in their own need, and God delights to care for those who care for others. Yet the Bible is full of generous, faithful people who were poor, and the New Testament praises a widow who gave all she had. This same chapter says a poor man with integrity is better than a rich man (verse 6), which shows that Proverbs does not measure faithfulness by wealth.

The verse means that giving is not a loss in God's economy, and that the one who hides his eyes from the poor stores up curses instead. It is not a way to get rich, and no one who has given and still struggles should think they gave wrongly.
passages.asks: The one who hides his eyes from the poor stores up curses. Ask where you have learned to look away. And ask whom you trust most, yourself or the LORD, since verse 26 calls trust in oneself folly.
